跟着在广岛读博的リュウ，去岛根山里的驾校合宿两周：集合出发、听规矩、第一次摸车、: Follow Liu, a PhD student in Hiroshima, to a two-week live-in course at a driving school in the mountains of Shimane: meeting up and setting off, hearing the rules, sitting in a real car for the first time, chatting with a roommate from Osaka, and working step by step toward a driver's license.
车站集合出发: Meeting up at the station and setting off
十一月的一个早上，广岛站前的巴士站。リュウ一个半月前报名了岛根山里「みどり台自動: A November morning at the bus stop in front of Hiroshima Station. A month and a half ago, Liu signed up for a two-week live-in course at 「みどり台自動車学校」 in the mountains of Shimane, and today is the day he starts. Quite a few young people with suitcases have already gathered at the bus stop: some from Tokyo, Fukuoka, and Okayama, and one who rushed over from Gifu early this morning.
主角，在广岛的大学读博士的中国留学生，三十岁左右，第一次学开车: The main character: a Chinese international student doing a PhD at a university in Hiroshima, around thirty, learning to drive for the first time
从东京来的女大学生，趁大学没课的空档来参加合宿，开朗爱说话: A university student from Tokyo who joined the live-in course during a break in her classes; cheerful and talkative
从岐阜来的二十出头的小伙子，早上五点就出门了: A young man in his early twenties from Gifu who left home at five this morning
彼此都是第一次见面的同期学员，年龄也差不多，用简单的丁宁语（です・ます）最合适。: They're fellow trainees in the same intake, meeting for the first time and about the same age, so simple polite (です/ます) style is the best fit. Among young people, casual expressions (「〜って」「〜ちゃって」「よろしくです」) soon start to creep in, but keeping your very first words a bit polite means you can't go wrong.
不好意思，请问绿台驾校合宿的集合地点是这里吗？: Excuse me, is this the meeting point for the Midoridai Driving School live-in course?
「〜って」是口语里的「〜は」，问路、确认时很常用，听起来比「〜は」轻松一点。对陌: 「〜って」 is the conversational version of 「〜は」. It's very common when asking the way or checking something, and it sounds a little more relaxed than 「〜は」. Saying 「すみません」 before you speak to a stranger lets them know you're about to ask something.
对，好像是这里。我也刚到。: Yes, it seems so. I just got here too.
自己也不太确定时，说「そうみたいです」（好像是），比斩钉截铁的「そうです」更诚实: When you aren't quite sure yourself, saying 「そうみたいです」 (it seems so) is more honest than a flat, definite 「そうです」. 「今来たところです」 = I've just arrived; it instantly closes the distance: we're in the same boat.
太好了。我从东京来的，刚才迷路了。: Oh, good. I came from Tokyo, and I got lost on the way.
从东京来的啊，好远。我住在广岛。: From Tokyo? That's far. I live in Hiroshima.
早上好。我是从岐阜来的，早上五点就出门了。: Good morning. I'm from Gifu. I left home at five this morning.
说实话，挺困的。不过一想到终于能拿驾照了，就很兴奋。: Honestly, I am sleepy. But when I think that I can finally get my license, I get so excited...
「〜と思うと」= 一想到……就……，后面接心情。「わくわく」是期待、兴奋得心里痒: 「〜と思うと」 = when I think that..., and it's followed by a feeling. 「わくわく」 is the tingly feeling of eager anticipation and excitement. Stopping the sentence halfway sounds more natural than finishing it.
刚才还有从福冈、冈山来的人。大家好像都坐同一辆巴士。: Earlier there were people from Fukuoka and Okayama, too. It looks like everyone's taking the same bus.
这两周请多关照，我叫由衣。: I look forward to the next two weeks with you all. I'm Yui.
合宿要一起住两周，日本人第一次见面会先说「よろしくお願いします」再报名字。只报名: Since everyone will be living together for two weeks, Japanese people meeting for the first time say 「よろしくお願いします」 before giving their name. Giving only your name without this phrase can come across as a little cold.
我叫刘。从中国来的，现在在读研究生院。请多关照。: I'm Liu. I came here from China, and now I'm studying at graduate school. Nice to meet you.
我叫健太。多关照！: I'm Kenta. Nice to meet ya!
「よろしくです」是年轻人之间的随意说法，介于「よろしく」和「よろしくお願いします: 「よろしくです」 is a casual expression used among young people, somewhere between 「よろしく」 and 「よろしくお願いします」. It's fine with people your own age, but with teachers and staff, say the full 「よろしくお願いします」.
啊，巴士来了。好像还在发便当。: Oh, the bus is here. Looks like they're handing out bento, too.
听说到那边要两个半小时。有便当，真是太好了。: I hear it takes two and a half hours to get there. It's so thoughtful of them to give us bento.
「〜そうです」接在动词原形后，表示「听说」，信息是从别人那里来的。「ありがたい」: 「〜そうです」 after the dictionary form of a verb means "I hear that...": the information came from someone else. 「ありがたい」 expresses gratitude for someone's consideration; compared with 「うれしい」, it carries more of a sense of "thank you for being so thoughtful."
那我吃完睡一会儿。到了叫醒我。: Then I'll sleep a bit after I eat. Please wake me up when we get there.
驾校的「合宿免許」是住在学校附近、两周左右集中学完拿驾照；社团的集训也叫合宿: At driving schools, 「合宿免許」 means living near the school and completing all the training for a license intensively in about two weeks; a club's training camp is also called 合宿
也说「教習所（きょうしゅうじょ）」，口语常简称「自動車校」: Also called 「教習所（きょうしゅうじょ）」; in casual speech often shortened to 「自動車校」
「集合場所」= 集合地点，「八時集合」= 八点集合: 「集合場所」 = meeting point, 「八時集合」 = meet at eight
「免許を取る」= 考到驾照；「運転免許」是正式说法: 「免許を取る」 = to get one's (driver's) license; 「運転免許」 is the formal term
「道に迷う」= 迷路；「どっちにするか迷う」= 拿不定主意: 「道に迷う」 = to lose one's way; 「どっちにするか迷う」 = to be torn about which to choose
放句首当副词：「正直、眠いです」；也说「正直に言うと」: Used as an adverb at the start of a sentence: 「正直、眠いです」; you can also say 「正直に言うと」
对将来的事充满期待；紧张不安是「どきどき」: Eager anticipation about something coming up; nervous, anxious excitement is 「どきどき」
「お弁当を配る」「資料を配る」；「気を配る」= 处处留心: 「お弁当を配る」「資料を配る」; 「気を配る」 = to be attentive to every detail
合宿、旅行常有人准备；「お」让说法更柔和有礼: Often provided on live-in courses and trips; the 「お」 makes the word softer and more polite
「駅に着く」；「着いたら連絡してね」= 到了联系我: 「駅に着く」; 「着いたら連絡してね」 = let me know when you get there
「七時に起こしてください」；自己醒来是「起きる」: 「七時に起こしてください」; waking up by yourself is 「起きる」
值得感激的: much appreciated, something to be grateful for
对别人的好意说「ありがたいです」，比「うれしい」多一份感谢: Said in response to someone's kindness: 「ありがたいです」; it carries more gratitude than 「うれしい」
好像……（根据看到、听到的推测）: it seems... (a guess based on what you see or hear)
名词／动词普通形 + みたいです: Noun / verb plain form + みたいです
自己看到了一些迹象、但不百分之百确定时用。日本人不喜欢把没把握的事说死，用「みた: Used when you've noticed some signs but aren't 100% sure. Japanese people don't like to state things they aren't sure of as fact; 「みたいです」 leaves a little leeway, so nobody is put in an awkward spot if you turn out to be wrong. It's more conversational than 「らしい」 and more casual than 「ようです」.
大家好像坐同一辆巴士。: It looks like everyone's taking the same bus.
那个人好像也是来参加合宿的。: That person seems to be on the live-in course, too.
好像在发便当。: It looks like they're handing out bento.
告诉别人自己从别处听来的信息。加上它，等于说「这不是我说的，是我听来的」，万一信: Used to pass on information you heard from somewhere else. Adding it is like saying "this isn't my own claim; it's something I heard," so if the information turns out to be off, it won't look like you were deceiving anyone. Note that it connects differently from the そう in 「おいしそうです」 (it looks delicious).
听说到学校要两个半小时。: I hear it takes two and a half hours to get to the school.
听说明天要下雪。: I hear it's going to snow tomorrow.
在集合地点、活动会场遇到陌生人，先用「すみません、〜って、ここですか」确认，再报: When you meet strangers at a meeting point or event venue, first check with 「すみません、〜って、ここですか」, then give your name and say 「よろしくお願いします」. Use 「みたいです」 for things you aren't sure of, and 「そうです」 for news you heard from others.
不要一上来就问对方年龄、工作、为什么要来，第一次见面先从「从哪里来」「坐什么来的: Don't open by asking someone's age, job, or why they came. When you first meet, start with easy topics like "Where are you from?" or "How did you get here?" Also, don't present something you heard as a plain 「〜です」: if it turns out to be wrong, the other person will feel you misled them.
合宿的人都是一个人来的，心里其实都有点不安。你先开口打招呼、说一句「我也刚到」，: Everyone on a live-in course has come alone, and deep down they're all a little anxious. If you speak first and say something like "I just got here too," the other person will feel relieved: "Thank goodness, someone's in the same boat as me." Two weeks together often begin with that very first line.
合宿的第一天，巴士站上全是不认识的人，大家各自看着手机，谁也不先开口。其实每个人: On the first day of the course, the bus stop is full of strangers, each looking at their own phone, and nobody speaks first. In fact, everyone is waiting for someone else to start. Yui asks, "Is this the meeting point?", Liu replies, "I just got here too," Kenta laughs and says he left home at five, and the three strangers hit it off right away. The same goes for the bento the driving school provides: one bento isn't expensive, but it makes people who've spent two and a half hours on a bus feel that "someone is looking out for us." Japanese people care a lot about this kind of small 「気配り」 (thoughtful consideration). When you notice someone's thoughtfulness, say so. A simple 「ありがたいですね」 makes the people who prepared it feel their effort was worth it.
在集合地点想确认「这里是不是驾校合宿的集合地点」，最自然的是？: At the meeting point, you want to check "Is this the meeting point for the driving school's live-in course?" What's the most natural way to ask?
先说「すみません」再问；「〜って」是轻松但不失礼的问法。「ございますか」太郑重，: Say 「すみません」 first, then ask; 「〜って」 is a relaxed way to ask that's still polite. 「ございますか」 is too formal: it sounds like a shop clerk talking.
司机告诉你到学校要两个半小时，你转告同伴时最合适的是？: The driver tells you it takes two and a half hours to get to the school. What's the best way to pass this on to the others?
信息是听来的，用传闻的「〜そうです」最准确。: You heard the information from someone else, so hearsay 「〜そうです」 is the most accurate.
对第一次见面、要一起住两周的同龄人自我介绍，哪句最好？: You're introducing yourself to someone your own age whom you're meeting for the first time and will live with for two weeks. Which is best?
报名字 + 「よろしくお願いします」是最稳妥的；「でございます」太郑重，「だ」又: Your name + 「よろしくお願いします」 is the safest choice; 「でございます」 is too formal, and 「だ」 is too casual.
